newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Kinshasa asks Swiss to widen probe on Mobutu funds.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa asks Swiss to widen probe on Mobutu funds.

text.p: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has asked Switzerland to widen its probe into embezzlement during the Mobutu era by blocking any funds allegedly stashed by 12 top aides including ex-ministers, officials said on Thursday.
Separately, Switzerland's highest court rejected an appeal by Mobutu Sese Seko against a police search last May of his huge home at Satigny near Lausanne.

Swiss media have speculated that documents were seized at the property in the lakeside city where he spent four months after undergoing surgery last August. However, Folco Galli, spokesman of the Federal Office of Police Matters, said none were found.

As the 66-year-old Mobutu, deposed last May, lies stricken with prostate cancer in Morocco, lawyers and bankers continue to express scepticism that he left behind fat bank accounts or other major holdings traceable in Switzerland.

But the government of Laurent Kabila is determined to track down state funds allegedly siphoned off during the 32-year rule of Mobutu, who is said to have amassed a fortune which once topped $4 billion.

Galli said the Swiss Federal Office of Police Matters would seek more information from the Kinshasa prosecutor Mongulu T'Apanage, who failed to list any specific banking details in the request of August 3.
This makes it impossible for Swiss authorities for now to block any bank accounts or other assets allegedly held by the 12 aides listed in his letter, according to the spokesman.
"We have received a second request for judicial assistance concerning not just Mobutu but 12 high-level collaborators," Galli told Reuters from Berne.
"There are ministers and advisers among them also suspected of having committed various offences against the patrimony. The prosecutor asks us to block all of their assets in Switzerland."
Galli was not able to provide any names on Kinshasa's list.
"But for the time being we cannot take any provisional measures. We are going to write to the prosecutor asking him to provide details so we can locate any assets," Galli said.
Since the Swiss cabinet froze all assets of Mobutu and his family on May 17 -- the day after he was ousted -- Swiss banks have notified Berne of only 4.8 million Swiss francs ($3.1 million) in funds.
This was the result of a formal government survey among more than 400 Swiss commercial banks after an initial request for judicial assistance from Kinshasa.

Following the request from the public prosecutor of Lumbumbashi -- who had joined the rebels then on the brink of toppling Mobutu -- the Swiss sealed the property at Savigny and ordered it not be sold pending further investigation.
The sprawling property itself is valued at some eight million Swiss francs. Mobutu says he inherited it from his former wife, who died in 1977.
In their decision made public on Thursday, the Federal Tribunal in Lausanne, the country's highest court, said the search had been legal.
Without revealing what was found, the three judges said that Mobutu's home could have contained documents important to the investigation which should not be lost.

"At the current stage of the procedure, one does not know how the former wife of the plaintiff -- from whom he claims to have inherited the property -- acquired the property at Savigny, and one cannot exclude that this acquisition is related to the facts motivating the request (for judicial assistance)."
The tribunal ordered Mobutu to pay 5,000 Swiss francs in court costs. His lawyer in Lausanne was not immediately available for comment.
